To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) the use of public interactive displays and mobile phones in a city can be successful in engaging the public in civic engagement; (b) mobile phone use is more successful than public interactive displays in engaging the public; (c) the use of the mobile phone is more successful in engaging the general public, but the use of the interactive public display is more successful in involving the local government; (d) the use of mobile phone is more effective than interactive public display for the public, but

1) the use of public interfaces for crowdsourcing public opinion is a promising approach to civic engagement; 2) the performance of public interfaces is affected by the type of interface and the nature of the interaction, and 3) the use of crowdsourcing public interfaces is affected both by the nature of the topic and the nature of public officials.

(1) public displays are the most effective way to engage citizens in public opinion gathering; (2) mobile phone interfaces are the least effective; and (3) Internet interfaces are the most effective when the target audience is well educated.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the design of public human interfaces for crowdsourcing public opinion.
how to make urban computing technologies work in the public domain, and what lessons we can learn from real-life experiments.
the use of pervasive technologies to enable civic engagement and to explore the potential of public interfaces to engage citizens in a city.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the technology works as intended, but that the public is still not ready to engage with city officials through these technologies.
the public is interested in interacting with city officials, but the current technologies are not yet mature enough for this task.
public interactive technologies can be used for crowdsourcing public opinion, but that there are several factors to be considered before deploying such technologies in the wild.
The main takeaway from our work is that
public displays and mobile phone technologies can be used to collect public opinion in a way that is both engaging for citizens and useful for city officials.
public displays can be used to engage the public in civic activities, but the public is also interested in the use of their own mobile phones and other personal devices.
the public is willing to engage with the city, and that the city is willing to engage the public, if the technologies are easy to use, and if the city is willing and able to act upon what is learned.
